rules.name: Many failed logons for one account from one source
rules.description: The number of failed logons (Security 4625) for the same account name and source address within the window reaches the threshold (default 10 in 10 minutes).
rules.rationale: Password guessing and spraying produce bursts of failed logons. Mistyped passwords, stale service credentials and vulnerability scanners produce the same pattern, so the threshold, grouping and source matter.
evidenceRequirements: Security log event 4625 (requires an elevated session or Event Log Readers membership)
rules.titleTemplate: {Count} failed logons for {Data.TargetUserName} from {Data.IpAddress} within {WindowMinutes} minutes
falsePositives: Users who mistyped a password or have stale saved credentials
Service accounts with an expired password
rules.recommendedNextStep: Check whether any 4624 success follows from the same source, the logon type and source address, and whether the account is local or domain. Review the account lockout state.
rules.remediation: If the activity is not approved, an authorized responder could block the source address and review the account after validating impact. This toolkit never changes the system; any action is a manual decision for an authorized responder after validation.
limitations: A burst of failures does not prove compromise. If the Security log was cleared or has rotated, earlier failures are not visible.

rules.name: Security event log was cleared
rules.description: Security event 1102 records that the Security audit log was cleared.
rules.rationale: Clearing the Security log removes evidence and is used by attackers, but administrators also clear logs for maintenance.
evidenceRequirements: Security log event 1102 (requires an elevated session or Event Log Readers membership)
falsePositives: Lab machines that are reset regularly
rules.recommendedNextStep: Identify the account (SubjectUserName), the logon session and what happened just before the event. Check for forwarded copies of the log in a SIEM.
rules.remediation: Preserve remaining logs and forward them centrally. This toolkit never changes the system; any action is a manual decision for an authorized responder after validation.

rules.name: Service installed with a suspicious path or command
rules.description: Security event 4697 records a service whose file name is in a user-writable path or matches a script, download or shell-wrapper pattern.
rules.rationale: Creating a service is a common persistence step, and the service file name shows what it launches.
evidenceRequirements: Security log event 4697 (requires elevation and the Security System Extension audit policy)
rules.titleTemplate: Service {Data.ServiceName} installed from a suspicious path or command
falsePositives: Software installers that register services from ProgramData or a temp folder during setup
rules.recommendedNextStep: Check the installing account and process, whether the service still exists (WTH-SVC findings) and what the binary does.
rules.remediation: If the service is not approved, an authorized responder could stop and disable it after preserving the binary. This toolkit never changes the system; any action is a manual decision for an authorized responder after validation.

rules.name: Scheduled task created with a suspicious command
rules.description: Security event 4698 records a new scheduled task whose definition contains a script or download pattern or a command in a user-writable path.
rules.rationale: The task definition in the event shows what the task will run, which helps catch persistence at creation time.
evidenceRequirements: Security log event 4698 (requires elevation and the Other Object Access Events audit policy)
rules.titleTemplate: Scheduled task {Data.TaskName} created with a suspicious command
falsePositives: Software installers and updaters that register tasks
rules.recommendedNextStep: Read the full task XML in the event, identify the creating account and session, and check whether the task still exists (WTH-TASK findings).
rules.remediation: If the task is not approved, an authorized responder could disable it after preserving the definition. This toolkit never changes the system; any action is a manual decision for an authorized responder after validation.

rules.name: Member added to the local Administrators group
rules.description: Security event 4732 records that a member was added to the built-in Administrators group (SID S-1-5-32-544).
rules.rationale: Adding an account to the Administrators group is a way to gain or keep privileged access. It is also a normal provisioning step, so authorization is what matters.
evidenceRequirements: Security log event 4732 (requires elevation and the Security Group Management audit policy)
falsePositives: IT provisioning and help desk changes
rules.recommendedNextStep: Confirm the change with the requester or ticket, identify the acting account and session, and review the new member's activity.
rules.remediation: If the change is not approved, an authorized administrator could remove the member after investigation. This toolkit never changes the system; any action is a manual decision for an authorized responder after validation.

rules.name: Suspicious content in PowerShell script block log
rules.description: A PowerShell script block (event 4104) contains a download cradle, AMSI tampering strings, reflective assembly loading, VirtualAlloc, or a Defender exclusion command.
rules.rationale: Script block logging records deobfuscated script text, so these strings are meaningful. Security tools and administrators can also contain them.
evidenceRequirements: PowerShell Operational event 4104 (script block logging must be enabled)
rules.titleTemplate: PowerShell script block {Data.ScriptBlockId} contains suspicious content
falsePositives: Security assessment and red-team tooling run with authorization
rules.recommendedNextStep: Read the full script block (and the other parts if it was split), and identify the user, host process and parent. Review related network and file activity.
rules.remediation: If the script is not approved, an authorized responder could contain the host after preserving logs. This toolkit never changes the system; any action is a manual decision for an authorized responder after validation.
limitations: Long script blocks are split across events; only the part that matched is evaluated per event.

rules.name: Sysmon process creation with an encoded PowerShell command
rules.description: Sysmon event 1 records a process whose command line contains an encoded PowerShell argument.
rules.rationale: Sysmon records every process start with its full command line, so short-lived processes are captured. Encoded commands need to be decoded and reviewed.
evidenceRequirements: Sysmon Operational event 1 (Sysmon must be installed with a process-create configuration)
rules.titleTemplate: Sysmon: {Data.Image} started with an encoded command
rules.recommendedNextStep: Decode the payload offline, check the parent image and user, and look for script block events (4104) for the same process.
rules.remediation: If the activity is not approved, an authorized responder could contain the host after preserving evidence. This toolkit never changes the system; any action is a manual decision for an authorized responder after validation.

rules.name: Sysmon: Office application started a script interpreter
rules.description: Sysmon event 1 shows an Office application as the parent of cmd.exe, PowerShell, a script host, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 or wmic.
rules.rationale: This relationship is a classic result of a malicious document. Sysmon captures short-lived children that a process snapshot would miss.
falsePositives: Office add-ins and automation that call cmd.exe or PowerShell
rules.recommendedNextStep: Identify the document, its source, the child command line and the user. Check for follow-on network and persistence activity.
rules.remediation: If the activity is not approved, an authorized responder could contain the host and preserve the document. This toolkit never changes the system; any action is a manual decision for an authorized responder after validation.

rules.name: Sysmon: Run key value set to a user-writable path
rules.description: Sysmon event 13 shows a Run or RunOnce registry value being set to data that points into a user-writable path.
rules.rationale: This catches the creation of Run-key persistence at the moment it happens, including the process that wrote it.
evidenceRequirements: Sysmon Operational event 13 (registry value set) with Run-key monitoring in the configuration
rules.titleTemplate: Sysmon: {Data.Image} set a Run value to a user-writable path
falsePositives: Per-user application installers registering autostart entries
rules.recommendedNextStep: Identify the writing process and user, verify the program the value points to, and check whether the entry still exists (WTH-REG findings).
rules.remediation: If the entry is not approved, an authorized responder could remove it after exporting the key. This toolkit never changes the system; any action is a manual decision for an authorized responder after validation.
